entryKnowledge: An organism is one living individual; a population is a group of individuals of the same species.
Plants consist of cells, and cells contain DNA.
Offspring are new individuals produced by reproduction. No chromosome terminology is assumed.

teaching.mainLearnerQuestion: How can reproduction keep a species going, while either copying a useful plant or producing inherited variation?
teaching.observableAction: Choose a reproductive starting group for a stated purpose and explain the choice using inherited DNA, copying or different inherited combinations, then bound the prediction.
teaching.structure: Concept through contrast, supported by one concrete runner example and one deliberately limited sexual cross. Revisit the grower's disease problem, then transfer to a dry-soil trial.
causalChain: A rooted daughter plant is a new individual, so reproduction can provide another generation even though a parent has a limited lifetime.
The daughter receives DNA from its parent. In runner reproduction, new cells copy the parent's DNA, so the daughter usually retains very similar inherited information.

In a sexual cross, sperm and egg join inside a flower and each contributes DNA. Different reproductive cells can carry different inherited selections, so joining different pairs can produce different offspring combinations even with the same two parents.

A copied plant can retain valued inherited characteristics and a shared inherited weakness. Different inherited combinations may give different responses to a changed condition, if the relevant differences are present.
Producing offspring permits continuity. Enough offspring still need to survive and reproduce for a population to continue.

scenes.heading: Copy a good plant. Then conditions change.
scenes.narration: Imagine you've grown a strawberry plant with the fruit you want. You can make new plants from it, so why start again with an uncertain result? Copying sounds useful. Then a new disease reaches the farm. Could those copies share a weakness as well as the fruit characteristics you wanted? To answer that, we need to follow what a new plant inherits.

scenes.role: Connect new individuals and inherited DNA to later generations
scenes.heading: A new plant can become a new parent.
scenes.narration: First, a plant growing more leaves is still the same individual. Reproduction makes another individual: an offspring. Here, the small plant has its own roots and leaves. Once established, it can grow separately, and later it can make offspring too. The original plant will not live for ever, but another generation can follow it. The new plant also receives DNA from its parent. DNA carries inherited information, information passed from parent to offspring, that helps shape the plant's characteristics. For the population to continue, enough offspring must survive and reproduce in turn.

scenes.role: Explain copying through the runner case before naming the method
scenes.heading: A runner keeps a useful inherited combination.
scenes.narration: The connecting stem is a runner. A new plant grows from it without a sperm cell and an egg cell joining. We call that asexual reproduction. As the new cells form, they copy the parent's DNA. The daughter usually has almost the same inherited information as its parent, so we call it a clone. That's why runners are useful to our grower: they can keep a valued inherited combination instead of mixing it with information from another plant. Similar DNA does not mean every plant grows exactly alike, because growing conditions still matter.

scenes.role: Introduce the minimum joining event with actual plants
scenes.heading: Sperm and egg join in sexual reproduction.
scenes.narration: A strawberry plant can also make offspring through a flower. Consider a cross between two genetically different plants, meaning their inherited DNA differs. Inside a flower of one parent, a sperm cell from the other joins an egg cell. Sperm and egg are reproductive cells called gametes. Each contributes DNA. Reproduction in which gametes join is called sexual reproduction. The developing new plant is inside a seed, and that seed can grow into a seedling. So the runner and this cross both produce new plants, but the cross brings inherited information from the two parents together.

scenes.role: Explain inherited variation without chromosome vocabulary
scenes.heading: Offspring can inherit different combinations.
scenes.narration: How can the same two parents produce different seedlings? Different sperm cells can carry different selections of one parent's inherited information. Egg cells can differ in the same way. When different pairs join, the seedlings can receive different combinations of DNA. Those differences in inherited information are genetic variation. Here is the contrast we need: runner offspring usually retain the parent's combination, while offspring from this cross can inherit different combinations. That gives the grower different plants to compare. It does not tell us which one will perform best.

Connect each possible joining event to its later recognisable seedling, then hold both possibilities together. The examples illustrate possibilities from the same parents, not observed offspring or an exhaustive set. scenes.role: Resolve the hook through the causal contrast
scenes.heading: A useful copy can share a weakness.
scenes.narration: Now return to the disease at the farm. The grower copied a plant because its inherited characteristics were useful. But if that plant also has an inherited weakness against the new disease, its clones may share it. That is a shared risk, not proof that every plant will become infected. Seedlings with different inherited combinations may respond differently, if the parents carry differences that matter for this disease. Copying helps keep a combination we already value. Sexual reproduction can offer different combinations to compare when conditions change. For this grower, a useful reminder is: copy to keep, cross to compare. The choice still depends on the conditions and the purpose.

Which group would you choose for this search? Explain your choice, then name one result you cannot predict yet. Pause here to decide.

scenes.role: Explain the choice and its limit one stage at a time
scenes.heading: Different combinations give a wider search.
scenes.narration: The crossed seedlings are the better starting group for a search for different inherited responses. They receive DNA through sexual reproduction from genetically different parents, so they can inherit different combinations. Runner offspring usually copy a much narrower set of inherited information from one parent. But we still cannot predict which seedling will grow well in the dry soil. The parents may not carry useful differences for that condition, and a particular seedling may not receive a useful combination. We would need to compare how the plants actually grow there. More variation gives us possibilities to investigate, not a promised winner.

scienceSources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: How strawberry plants grow
scienceSources.supports: Runners connect the parent crown to rooted daughter plants. Leaf and root structures are appropriate physical anchors. The lesson does not import Minnesota cultivation timings.

scienceSources.title: University of Florida IFAS: The Strawberry Clean Plant Program
scienceSources.supports: New strawberry hybrids are propagated by seed and selected seedlings are subsequently propagated vegetatively by runners. Breeding, runner multiplication, pathogen testing and later performance verification are distinct steps. This supports the concrete copying-versus-search context without asserting disease outcomes for every clone.

scienceSources.supports: Strawberry varieties can differ in response to water limitation. The transfer is a fictional decision under supplied unknown outcomes, not a claim that untested crossed seedlings are drought tolerant or that this study proves a reproductive-method comparison.

authorOnlyScienceNotes: Usually and can are deliberate qualifiers. Do not replace them with all clones are identical or every sexual offspring is different. Mutation can introduce DNA differences in clonal descendants; it is outside this video's primary question and needs no new definition here.

A difference in plant appearance is not proof of genetic variation. Growing conditions affect phenotype. The stated reproductive origins and genetically different parents supply the inheritance comparison, not the painted seedling appearance.

Genetic differences need not affect the disease or dry-soil response under discussion. Shared susceptibility does not establish infection, infection count or mortality. Exposure, pathogen and growing conditions also matter; these are not a new disease lecture in this opening lesson.

Seed formation is restricted to the stated sexual cross. Apomixis and self-fertilisation are genuine exceptions to simplified parent-count or seed heuristics, but the proposal makes neither heuristic a general classification rule.

Sperm and egg each contribute DNA. Do not imply that the physical cells are two equal volumes poured together, that pollen itself is the sperm, or that joining reproductive cells instantaneously creates an adult plant.

Neither a clone crop nor a sexually produced group guarantees sufficient surviving and reproducing descendants. Continuity is an enabled possibility and a population-level requirement, not a promised survival result.

Actual recording and pilot review must confirm that each new term is understood in its concrete scene. Source authoring cannot claim that a student has learned the term or successfully transferred the reasoning.
